etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Attested since the 1500s in the sense "indulged child" and since the 1530s in the sense "animal companion". From Scots and dialectal Northern English, of unclear origin. Perhaps a back-formation of petty, pety (“little, small”), a term formerly used to describe children and animals (e.g. pet lambs). Alternatively, perhaps a borrowing of Scottish Gaelic peata, from Middle Irish petta, peta (“pet, lap-dog”), of uncertain (possibly pre-Indo-European substrate) origin. Compare peat (“pet, darling, woman”).

The verb is derived from the noun.

definitions.definition: An animal kept as a companion.
(by extension) Something kept as a companion, including inanimate objects. (pet rock, pet plant, etc.)

quote.citation: 2015 September 15, Toby Fox, Undertale, Linux, Microsoft Windows, OS X:
quote.text: Papyrus: This is my brother's pet rock. He always forgets to feed it. As usual, I have to take responsibility.

definitions.definition: One who is excessively loyal to a superior and receives preferential treatment.
Any person or animal especially cherished and indulged; a darling.

quote.citation: 1847 December, Ellis Bell [pseudonym; Emily Brontë], chapter XIX, in Wuthering Heights: […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Thomas Cautley Newby, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: At first she sat silent; but that could not last: she had resolved to make a pet of her little cousin, as she would have him to be; and she commenced stroking his curls, and kissing his cheek, and offering him tea in her saucer, like a baby.

quote.citation: 1711 January 1 (Gregorian calendar), Isaac Bickerstaff [et al., pseudonyms; Richard Steele et al.], “Thursday, December 21, 1710”, in The Tatler, number 266; republished in [Richard Steele], editor, The Tatler, […], London stereotype edition, volume III, London: I. Walker and Co.;  […], 1822, →OCLC:
quote.text: the love of cronies, pets, and favouritesThe spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive, informal) To stroke or fondle (another person) amorously.

quote.citation: 1970-1975, Lou Sullivan, personal diary, quoted in 2019, Ellis Martin, Zach Ozma (editors), We Both Laughed In Pleasure
quote.text: We kissed & petted for about 15 mins & he still wasn't hard, altho he acted like he was enjoying himself.

definitions.definition: (dated, transitive) To treat as a pet; to fondle; to indulge.

quote.citation: 1919 August, P. G. Wodehouse, “Prohibition and the Drama”, in Vanity Fair, page 21:
quote.text: […]  the American dramatist has had to waste most of his first act elaborately planting the information that his Mister Quex is rich, petted by Society, and altogether more spectacular than the common run of men.

definitions.definition: (archaic, intransitive) To be peevish; to sulk.

quote.citation: 1623, Owen Feltham, Resolves: Divine, Moral, Political:
quote.text: He sure is queasie stomach't that must pet, and puke, at such a trivial circumstance

definitions.definition: Favourite; cherished; the focus of one's (usually positive) attention.

quote.citation: 1886, Frederic Harrison, The Choice of Books:
1875, William Conant Church, The Galaxy, page 141:
quote.text: Major Butler has a pet grievance and a pet aversion, which he forces on the  reader in every chapter, and which becomes at last very wearisome.

quote.citation: 1991, Deborah G. Douglas, United States Women in Aviation, 1940-1985, page 9:
quote.text: In an interview with Flying magazine, Heberding commented that her pet annoyance was "the reluctance of people generally to accept a woman whether as a pilot or a preflight inspector."

definitions.definition: Kept or treated as a pet.

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Now,” said Hands, “look there; there’s a pet bit for to beach a ship in. Fine flat sand, never a cat's paw, trees all around of it, and flowers a-blowing like a garding on that old ship.”

definitions.definition: A fit of petulance, a sulk, arising from the impression that one has been offended or slighted.

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 3, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849–1850, →OCLC:
quote.text: His genius at this time was of a decidedly gloomy cast. He brought his mother a tragedy, in which, though he killed sixteen people before the second act, it made her laugh so, that he thrust the masterpiece into the fire in a pet.

quote.citation: 1891, Mary Noailles Murfree, In the "Stranger People's" Country, Nebraska, published 2005, page 105:
quote.text: There was something ludicrous, even more, unbecoming a gentleman, in leaving a friend's house in a pet, with the host's reproaches sounding in his ears, to be matched only by the bitterness of the guest's sneering retorts.

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[Episode 1]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Buck Mulligan sat down in a sudden pet.

definitions.definition: (Ireland, Geordie) A term of endearment usually applied to women and children.
